# Introduction: Why the "AI/ML Workflow" Axis?

The essence of O-RAN lies in disaggregating base stations and 
opening them up to standard interfaces, but the **purpose** of its existence 
is to enable the deployment of ML to RAN control. Therefore, if O-RAN 
is viewed not as "disaggregating boxes" but as a matter of **"how to place an ML pipeline on which node of the network"**, 
the architecture, interfaces, and deployment scenarios align into a single consistent picture.

From this perspective, the core questions can be condensed into two.

1. What **functional stages** make up an AI/ML workflow?
2. Each step **which node (SMO / Non-RT RIC / Near-RT RIC / RAN node)**
can be placed at |||, and what is the constraint that determines the choice?

The decisive variable determining the answer to the second question is **timescale** 
, and this is the axis that runs through the entire document.

# Background: O-RAN control layer hosting AI/ML

we organize the control layer that defines "where" the workflow is placed based on the time scale.

| Hierarchy | Timescale | Hosting Unit | Interface | Primary Role |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| SMO / Non-RT RIC | > 1 s | rApp | A1, O1, O2 | Policy/Model Management, Training, Intent Management |
| Near-RT RIC | 10 ms – 1 s | xApp | E2 | Real-time RRM control, inference |
| RAN node (CU/DU) | < 10 ms | (embedded) | — | Real-time control such as scheduling and HARQ |

: Timescale layer of O-RAN control loop {#tbl-timescale}

If this hierarchical structure is formalized as a nested control loop, 
the outer loop is slower and global, while the inner loop is faster and local. 
When the control cycle is denoted as $T_\ell$, approximately

$$
T_{\text{Non-RT}} \;>\; 1\,\text{s}
\;\gg\;
T_{\text{Near-RT}} \in [10\,\text{ms},\,1\,\text{s}]
\;\gg\;
T_{\text{RT}} \;<\; 10\,\text{ms}
$$

holds. **<10 ms real-time loops are 
an area not standardized in the current specification (further study),** and this fact is directly related to the subsequent research gap.

# Lifecycle Stages of AI/ML Workflow

The AI/ML lifecycle defined by O-RAN WG2 
is a cyclic pipeline from data to inference, consisting of the following stages.

1. **Data Preparation** — Collection · Preprocessing · Feature Engineering
2. **AI/ML Training** — Model Training (Offline is generally required)
3. **Validation & Deployment** — Deploy to target nodes after validation
4. **Inference** — Perform real-time inference with a trained model
5. **Continuous Operations** — Post-deployment performance monitoring and retraining triggers

The core operating principles are as follows.

- **Offline training required**: Discontinue the discontinuation of unverified models.
Online learning is permitted only for fine-tuning purposes.
- **Current Limit of Inference Host**: Inference is limited to **RIC** in the current specification, and
Inference in CU/DU is in a pending (further study) state.

# Node Deployment of Workflow Function: Deployment Scenario (Fig. 14)

Fig. 14 of the paper classifies the above workflow 
into five scenarios based on which node the five function columns 
(Model Management / Continuous Operations / Data Preparation / Training / Inference) are placed 
. Since this is the key table of this document, it is summarized in detail.

## Function placement by scenario

| Scenario | Model Mgmt | Continuous Ops | Data Prep | Training | Inference |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **1.1** | Non-RT | Non-RT | Non-RT | Non-RT | Non-RT |
| **1.2** | SMO | Non-RT | Non-RT / Near-RT | Non-RT | **Near-RT** |
| **1.3** | SMO | Non-RT | SMO | SMO | Non-RT |
| **1.4** | Non-RT | **Near-RT** | Non-RT | Non-RT / SMO | **Near-RT** |
| **1.5 (FFS)** | Non-RT | (Undetermined) | (Undetermined) | (Undetermined) | **O-CU / O-DU** |

: O-RAN AI/ML Deployment Scenario (Fig. 14 reconfigured) {#tbl-scenarios}

## Scenario Interpretation

- **1.1 — Fully Centralized**: All functions concentrated in a Non-RT RIC. Inference
  >Since it is on a 1 s scale, it is suitable for slow decisions such as slicing policies and traffic forecasting.
Fast closed-loop control impossible.

- **1.2 — Separation of Training/Inference**: Training is Non-RT (Offline), **Inference is Near-RT**
descends to form a 10 ms–1 s closed loop. The most commonly discussed structure.

- **1.3 — Separation of Authority**: Model Management and Training are owned by **SMO**,
Operation and inference are handled by Non-RT. 
A structure in which a central SMO deploys a common model in a large-scale network and local Non-RTs perform inference.

- **1.4 — Online Adaptive Loop**: Unlike 1.2, up to **Continuous Operations**
Near-RT** is in charge. The model self-monitors in real-time and 
requests retraining from Non-RT if performance degrades. It has the highest responsiveness among RIC-based scenarios.

- **1.5 (FFS) — RAN Node Inference**: **Inference is executed on the O-CU/O-DU itself**.
The only structure that enables real-time control of the TTI scale, 
but is **not yet standardized (For Further Study)**.

> **How to Read**: In Scenario 1.5, which of the SMO·Near-RT RICs is empty in the table
> It is not "not needed", but rather **since it is FFS, the placement of that function is simply undefined**.
> Two controllers are always present in the network for FCAPS management, RRM, etc.

# Chained AI/ML Models and Data Access Platform

emphasizes that 
the workflow can be configured using **model chaining** rather than a single model . The inference output of one model 
becomes the input of another model, and a data access platform (middleware) mediates the production/consumption of this.

Representative example (based on papers):

$$
\underbrace{\text{rApp: 트래픽 예측}}_{A}
\;\rightarrow\;
\underbrace{\text{xApp Y: 슬라이싱 프로파일}}_{C}
\;\rightarrow\;
\underbrace{\text{xApp Z: 스케줄링 프로파일}}_{D \,=\, f(A,\,B_{\text{KPM}},\,C)}
$$

This structure 
illustrates a hierarchical information flow where **slow prediction (upper) sets the input for fast scheduling (lower)**, leading to the subsequent discussion on hierarchical design.

# Use Cases Where ML Is Actually Applied

Among the ML application areas classified by the paper, the key points from the perspective of resource control are as follows.

- **Resource Allocation** (Network Slicing/Scheduling) — ML Application
Most active area. Numerous closed-loop slicing control examples (ColO-RAN, NexRAN, etc.).
- **Mobility** — Handover/Load Balancing Prediction.
- **QoE/QoS Control** — Resource adjustment based on user perceived quality.
- **RAN Sharing / Massive MIMO / New Applications**(UAV·Vehicle·Industrial IoT).

Among these, **scheduling** is the region with the fastest time scale, so 
it is highlighted that only **1.5 (in-node inference)** is timing-appropriate in the scenario table above.

# Research Gap {#sec-gaps}

We address the gaps explicitly and implicitly left by the paper from the perspective of AI/ML workflow. 
Everything converges around **Scenario 1.5 (In-node Inference)**.

## Gap 1 — Real-time (<10 ms) Absence of inference loop

Since the inference host is limited to RIC (≥10 ms), 
there is no standard path to directly apply ML to **fast control at the TTI scale** (scheduling, link adaptation). 
Formally, for in-node inference to be possible, 
the sum of the inference delay $\tau_{\text{inf}}$ and the scheduling processing delay $\tau_{\text{sched}}$ must not exceed the TTI budget 
.

$$
\tau_{\text{inf}} + \tau_{\text{sched}} \;\le\; \text{TTI}
\quad (\text{TTI} \approx 0.5\text{–}1\,\text{ms})
$$

It is not verified whether this inequality holds in the current hardware and model structure, and 
this is the first technical reason why 1.5 is FFS.

## Gap 2 — Absence of model delivery interface

the 1.5 architecture where "Model Management is Non-RT and Inference is O-DU," a 
**standard interface to directly drop trained model weights from Non-RT to the node 
** is required. However, the current interface serves a different purpose.

| Interface | Design Purpose | Model Deployment Suitability |
|---|---|---|
| A1 | Policy·enrichment delivery | Partial |
| E2 | RRM Control Command | Non-conforming (Not for Model File Transfer) |
| O1 | FCAPS Management | Non-conformity |

: Standard space in model deployment path {#tbl-delivery}

## Gap 3 — Resource isolation

In-node inference implies that RAN functions and ML workloads **share the same hardware** 
. Consequently, (i) contention for GPU/CPU resources, (ii) 
jitter that undermines RAN real-time performance, and (iii) the absence of QoS-guaranteed resource allocation policies remain issues . 
A structure for **dynamic separation and allocation of RAN workloads and AI inference workloads** has not been defined.

## Gap 4 — Lack of utilization of cross-layer signals

Cross-layer mapping that propagates 
signals from model layers (e.g., token importance of generative models — entropy, logprob, attention) as **utility inputs to MAC schedulers** 
is an area rarely covered in either standards or literature. This 
gains significance when combined with Gap 1 (fast control + model-derived signals).

# Summary: Alignment to research positioning

The gaps above converge on a single axis called the **unrealized scenario 1.5**, and research demonstrating this naturally 
organizes into **hierarchical control** .

```
Non-RT RIC   →  트래픽 패턴 학습 / 중요도 prior 모델 관리   (> 1 s)
     │ A1
Near-RT RIC  →  채널·트래픽 예측 / 슬라이스 정책 조정      (10 ms–1 s)
     │ E2
O-DU (cuMAC) →  추론 + 토큰중요도 기반 PRB 할당 실행        (< 10 ms)
```

- **The Slow Layer (RIC)** supplies policies, weights, and predictions to the Fast Layer.
- **Fast layer (node)** directly executes inference + scheduling at the TTI scale.

In this structure, the systematic contribution of the study 
lies in the third row — the inference + scheduling loop that actually runs at the node — which 
corresponds to the first demonstration of 1.5 remaining as FFS. The necessary technical elements (channel quality prediction, traffic prediction) are 
each mapped as inputs to the Near-RT layer, and the verification environment (GH200 / pyAerial / cuMAC / 
ROS2) is mapped as the actual answer for Gap 1·3.

| Research Gap | Corresponding Factors | Verification Methods |
|---|---|---|
| Gap 1 (real-time inference) | sub-ms inference feasibility | GH200 + pyAerial measured |
| Gap 3 (Resource Isolation) | RAN+AI Workload Coexistence | Aerial Dynamic Allocation |
| Gap 4 (cross-layer signal) | Token Importance → Utility Input | cuMAC Scheduler |
| Prediction Factors | Channel/Traffic Prediction | Near-RT Layer Model |

: Mapping of Research Gap and Research Factors {#tbl-mapping}

# One-line summary

> The O-RAN AI/ML workflow is a problem of deploying 5 functions to 4 nodes, and
> The variable that determines that choice is the time scale. **Descending inference to the RAN node
> Only Scenario 1.5 enables TTI scale control, but it still remains as FFS.
> exists**, and precisely this unrealized point is cross-layer·systems-level research
> It is the core void to be placed.
